$comment: Shared calculation test vectors for the Kopnutera wallet engine.
The same logic exists twice: once in PHP (app/Domain/Rules/WalletCalculator.php)
and once in Dart (the Flutter app's domain layer). Nothing structurally prevents
the two from disagreeing after a fix lands on one side only.
This file is the shared contract. Both test suites read it and assert against it,
so a divergence fails CI on whichever side introduced it instead of surfacing as a
COPY THIS FILE INTO THE FLUTTER REPO (or wire it up as a git submodule). When you
add a case here, add it there in the same commit.
All money is whole IDR. The limit unlock floors. There is no rounding on the
fee side at all: a band charges a whole number of rupiah.
There is no salary and no access-cap percentage. Each employee has a
withdrawal_limit — the whole amount they may draw across one cycle — which
unlocks evenly across the cycle's days.
The fee is NOT a percentage. It is a ladder of flat bands (`fee_schedule`
below), and a band charges what it charges — there is no rounding left in it.
`max_withdrawal_amount` is the employer's ceiling. It clips the limit BEFORE
the daily unlock is worked out, so it changes the daily rate too. A vector
that omits it is asserting the uncapped behaviour.

pay_periods.name: the walkthrough from the plan — the 27th with a 25th cutoff is day 2
pay_periods.$note: 27 > 25, so the new cycle opened on the 26th of this month. Exactly 2 days of salary accrued, whatever the cycle length works out to.

pay_periods.name: cutoff day itself belongs to the CLOSING period
year boundary — cycle opened in December, closing in January
cutoff 28 in a non-leap February — no 29th to start on, so the cycle opens on 1 March
pay_periods.$note: This is the edge case the original plan did not cover. Neither a gap nor an overlap: the previous cycle ended 28 February.

pay_periods.name: new hire mid-cycle — elapsed days count from the join date
pay_periods.$note: total_days stays the FULL cycle so the daily rate matches what payroll pays per day. Only accrual is clipped.

pay_periods.name: join date before the cycle — no effect
joins today — one day elapsed, not zero
joins later this cycle — nothing earned yet

max_withdrawable.name: nothing withdrawn yet, half the cycle elapsed
prior withdrawal reduces what is left
a smaller limit simply unlocks more slowly
max_withdrawable.$note: Replaces the old 50%-access-cap vector. There is no cap percentage any more — halving the limit is how you halve the access, and it lands on the same number.

max_withdrawable.name: already past what has unlocked — clamps to zero, never negative
limit that does not divide evenly — daily rate floors
max_withdrawable.$note: 7000000/30 = 233333.33 -> floors to 233333. Flooring is deliberate: releasing the extra 0.33/day is money the employer cannot deduct back.

max_withdrawable.name: flooring again at a smaller magnitude
max_withdrawable.$note: 1000000/30 = 33333.33 -> 33333. The lost fraction scales with the cycle, not the limit, so a small limit loses proportionally more. Accepted: erring downward is the safe direction.

max_withdrawable.name: first day of a cycle — exactly one day unlocked
new hire mid-cycle unlocks from the join date only
max_withdrawable.$note: The daily rate still comes from the FULL cycle length, not the days remaining — only the elapsed count is clipped to the join date.

max_withdrawable.name: the employer ceiling clips the limit before anything else
max_withdrawable.$note: 5000000/30 = 166666.67 -> 166666, NOT 9000000/30. The ceiling is applied to the limit, not to the answer: capping only max_withdrawable would show this employee a daily rate of 300000 they could never actually draw.

max_withdrawable.name: a limit under the ceiling behaves as if there were none
the ceiling is per cycle, not per request
max_withdrawable.$note: Last day of the cycle, the whole ceiling drawn. Nothing left — an employee on a 9000000 limit does not get a second 5000000 after the first.

$fee_schedule_comment: The published fee table, and the platform default. Only each band's UPPER
bound is written down: a band starts one rupiah above the previous band's
upper bound, which is what makes a gap or an overlap impossible to express.
A fee case may carry its own `fee_tiers` to override this.

fees.name: bottom of the first band
fees.$note: Rp 50.000 is the smallest amount anyone may request, so this is the cheapest real advance there is.

fees.name: exactly on the first band's upper bound
fees.$note: Bands are inclusive at BOTH ends. The boundary belongs to the band below it, which is what the published table says: 'Rp 0 – Rp 100.000'.

fees.name: one rupiah over a boundary crosses into the next band
fees.$note: The whole point of the shape: Rp 1 more principal costs Rp 7.500 more fee. Off-by-one here is the most expensive bug available, on both sides.

fees.name: middle of a band charges the band, not a rate
fees.$note: 5% would be Rp 20.000 here by coincidence. Rp 260.000 in the same band is also Rp 20.000 — that is the difference.

fees.name: the million band
fees.$note: Was Rp 50.000 under the old flat 5%. The tiered table is cheaper here and dearer in the small bands.

fees.name: the top band, at its ceiling
fees.$note: Also the default max_withdrawal_amount. The table has to reach at least the ceiling or an amount in between has no price at all.

fees.name: zero amount is free whatever the first band says
fees.$note: The first band starts at 0 and charges Rp 5.000, but nothing withdrawn is nothing charged. The zero check comes first.

fees.name: above the top band has no price — this must THROW, not fall back
fees.$note: Falling back to the top band would undercharge silently and forever. Both implementations must refuse. Unreachable in practice: the ceiling caps the request first.

fees.name: an open-ended top band prices anything above it
fees.$note: Leaving the last upper bound empty is how an employer opts out of the ceiling check. Only the LAST band may be open-ended.

fees.name: a zero-fee employer
fees.$note: One open-ended band charging nothing. An empty table is NOT how you say this — that is rejected, because a table with no bands cannot price anything.

$effective_limit_comment: The employer ceiling clipping the roster limit. Applied before the daily
unlock, so it changes the daily rate — a Rp 8.000.000 limit under a
Rp 5.000.000 ceiling behaves exactly like a Rp 5.000.000 limit, not like a
Rp 8.000.000 limit with a per-request cap bolted on.

effective_limits.name: a limit under the ceiling is untouched
a limit over the ceiling is clipped to it
no ceiling configured leaves the limit alone
